alcohol.line: Alcohol is a depressant: a drug that slows the signals the brain and body send each other.
alcohol.note: Anchor confirmed word for word (ADF, 'What is alcohol?'). The line repeats ADF's stock family sentence (ten of its words in a row: 'it slows down the messages travelling between the brain and'), so it is reworded in our own words; the meaning is unchanged. Only one publisher (ADF) supports the family word here.
FRANK carries the whole line (ethanol or ethyl alcohol); the ADF sentence supports 'ethanol' only.
Longest runs shared with ADF are four and five words ('fermented or brewed liquid'; 'beer, wine, cider or spirits'), from two different sentences: kept. 'Cider' rests on ADF only.

ADF list after 'You may experience:' has 'feeling relaxed' and 'increased confidence and energy'; FRANK has 'more sociable' (after 'Some effects include:' in 'How does it make you feel?') and 'Sociable, chatty, relaxed' in Quick info.

alkyl-nitrites-and-inhalants.note: All five anchors confirmed. The line keeps the shape of ADF's definition and five of its words in a row ('household, industrial and medical products'): under the six-word mark, so kept, but it is the closest of this drug's lines to a source sentence. The first line describes inhalants as a group; alkyl nitrites follow in the second line, which is enough for someone who only knows the names.

ADF's sentences carry footnote numbers after the quoted words; EUDA prints 'poppers' in curly quotation marks. FRANK's page heading is 'alkyl nitrites' (browser title 'Poppers | Effects of Poppers | FRANK').

FRANK hedges ('giving some users'); the line's 'can give' keeps the hedge. The NIDA entry 'Volatile Solvents' is in the last part of the long A to Z page (read from character 100000); the same sentence also stands under 'Gases'. Two ideas in one line (poppers; solvents and gases), because the page groups them.
The first half is close to EUDA's clause ('Amyl nitrite is used as a first aid treatment for cyanide poisoning'): longest shared run four words, and the fact has few other plain wordings, so kept.

caffeine.line: Caffeine is a stimulant: it makes the brain and body pass messages to each other faster.
caffeine.note: Both anchors confirmed (ADF 'What is caffeine?'; MedlinePlus introduction: 'a central nervous system stimulant'). The line repeats ADF's stock family sentence (twelve of its words in a row: 'it speeds up the messages travelling between the brain and the body'), so it is reworded in our own words; the meaning is unchanged.

On ADF 'What does caffeine look like?' is a sub-heading under 'What is caffeine?', as the anchor says. The first half is near MedlinePlus's sentence (five words in a row: 'in the leaves, seeds and'), with 'nuts' and 'many plants' taken from ADF: under the six-word mark, kept.
ADF list item 'feeling more alert and active' (under 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:'); MedlinePlus 'Function' gives the short-term relief of fatigue or drowsiness.

ADF table lists espresso, caffeinated beverage or energy drink, instant coffee, black tea, cola drinks, milk chocolate; MedlinePlus 'Food Sources' lists coffee, tea, chocolate, most colas and 'Candies, energy drinks, snacks, gum'. MedlinePlus would not print its two sections in full, so each passage was asked for and read separately.

cocaine.line: Cocaine is a stimulant made from coca leaves; coca is a plant native to South America.
cocaine.note: All five anchors confirmed. The line is NIDA's sentence with its opening changed ('It is made from the leaves of the coca plant (Erythroxylon coca), which is native to South America': eight words in a row, then six more after the Latin name), so it is reworded; it says the same and no more.

ADF list: happiness, increased confidence, feeling energetic and alert; FRANK list after 'Taking cocaine can make you feel:': happy, excited, wide awake, confident; NIDA: 'Small amounts of cocaine usually make people feel euphoric, energetic, talkative, and mentally alert'.
FRANK carries the whole line (three types: coke, crack and freebase; fine white powder; small lumps or rocks). ADF describes crack as crystals and freebase as a white powder.

NIDA: 'can be administered by a doctor for medical uses, such as local anesthesia for some eye, ear, and throat surgeries' (five words in a row shared: 'some eye, ear and throat'); EUDA: limited medical use as a topical anaesthetic for surgery of the eye, ear, nose and throat.

dmt-ayahuasca.line: DMT is a psychedelic found in various plants; made in a lab, it is a white crystalline powder.
dmt-ayahuasca.note: All five anchors confirmed (ADF's DMT page shows 'Last updated: 13 Nov 2026'). The line strings together two source clauses word for word: 'found in a variety of plants' (six words in a row, ADF) and 'lab-made DMT is a white crystalline powder' (NIDA's clause without one bracketed word), so it is reworded; it says the same and no more. The family word 'psychedelic' is explained by the fourth line.

ADF: brew made by boiling the stems of one plant with the leaves of another, the second containing DMT; NIDA (A to Z, 'Ayahuasca'; and the DMT item under 'Psychedelic Drugs'): a tea. Longest shared runs four words.
ADF names Peru, Brazil, Colombia and Ecuador; NIDA says 'indigenous South Americans of the Amazon for religious and healing rituals'. In our own words.

dmt-ayahuasca.line: Both can change how people sense things, think and feel, and how time seems to pass.
dmt-ayahuasca.note: All four anchors confirmed (FRANK's Tryptamines page names DMT and ayahuasca in its 'Also called' line). The line is ADF's stock sentence for the psychedelic family, lightly rearranged ('can affect all the senses': five words in a row, then the same three items); ADF repeats it on its psychedelic pages, so it is reworded in our own words.

fentanyl-and-analogues.note: ADF: 'Fentanyl is a potent synthetic opioid.'; NIDA: 'synthetic, which means it is made entirely in laboratories'; NIDA A to Z: 'powerful synthetic (lab-made) opioid'; FRANK's page heading is 'New Synthetic opioids' and lists fentanyl under 'Also called'. Longest shared runs four words. 'Potent' is the sources' word; 'strong' would be plainer.

The list of forms follows ADF's ('patches, lollipops or lozenges, tablets, sprays and injections': five words in a row shared), under the six-word mark; ADF and FRANK say these are the forms of the medicine.

EUDA: fentanyl and its derivatives (alfentanil, sufentanil, remifentanil, carfentanil) are used as anaesthetics and analgesics; a range of non-pharmaceutical derivatives exists. FRANK's sentence stands in the introduction under the page heading, before 'Important'. In our own words; 'derivatives' is EUDA's term.

fentanyl-and-analogues.line: As other opioids do, it can relieve pain, and people can feel happy and relaxed.
fentanyl-and-analogues.note: All three anchors confirmed. The line is NIDA's sentence with two words changed ('Like other opioids, fentanyl can ease pain and make a person feel happy and relaxed.'), so it is reworded; ADF ('pain relief'; 'pleasure, feelings of happiness (euphoria)') and FRANK ('pain relief', 'euphoria or well-being', 'relaxation') support the same.

mdma.note: NIDA: 'a lab-made (synthetic) drug that has effects similar to stimulants like methamphetamine' (four words in a row shared); ADF: 'MDMA is an empathogen.' The first line leans on the family word 'empathogen', which someone who has only heard the name will not know; the second line explains it (closer and warmer towards other people), so the two lines together do the job.

NIDA: 'Effects include feeling happy, energetic, alert, and closer to others.'; ADF: empathy and kindness towards others; FRANK list after 'Most people feel:': 'loved up' (love and affection for the people they're with), 'energised and alert'. The line follows the order of NIDA's list but shares no run longer than three words.
ADF: crystal, powder, pills or capsules; names molly, ecstasy. FRANK: pill or powder; 'MDMA, mandy or MD'. NIDA: 'Molly' or 'Ecstasy'.

mdma.line: Researchers are studying therapy with MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder; in clinical settings it may help reduce hard-to-treat symptoms.
mdma.note: All three anchors confirmed. The second half says a little more than ADF, whose sentence ends '...the symptoms of treatment-resistant post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)': the line dropped 'treatment-resistant', so the corrected line keeps that limit in plain words. NIDA's first anchor says 'people with severe PTSD'; its second says research trials for depression and PTSD, which carries the first half as written. No source says MDMA is an approved medicine, and the line does not say so.

nicotine.line: Nicotine is a stimulant that occurs naturally in the tobacco plant; laboratories can also make it.
nicotine.note: All six anchors confirmed. The second half is ADF's sentence word for word ('It can also be made in a lab': eight words in a row; NIDA has the same sentence with 'laboratory'), so the line is reworded; it says the same and no more. 'Stimulant' is not explained here; the third line gives the feeling.
ADF Tobacco: nicotine 'is responsible for its stimulant effects'; dried leaves of the tobacco plant; FRANK Tobacco: leaves picked, dried and rubbed. In our own words.
ADF list under 'Effects of nicotine': 'increased alertness', 'increased energy'; FRANK: 'the buzz you feel is the release of adrenaline which stimulates the body' (said of inhaled nicotine).

FRANK's list under 'How do people take it?' and its introduction carry the whole line; ADF adds that approved nicotine replacement therapies are legal medicines ('Approved NRTs' is a heading low on the page, after 'Getting help'). Longest shared run four words ('help people stop smoking').

nitrous-oxide.line: Nitrous oxide, a colourless gas, is a dissociative: people can feel cut off from their body or surroundings.
nitrous-oxide.note: All four anchors confirmed (ADF's own sentence reads 'Nitrous oxide dissociative drug, which means...', with words missing on the page, as quoted). The line opens with six words found word for word on ADF and FRANK ('Nitrous oxide is a colourless gas') and then keeps the turn of phrase of ADF's stock sentence for dissociatives ('feel separated or detached from their body or physical environment': five words in a row), which also shows in the ketamine lines; reworded lightly in our own words, same meaning.

ADF list ('The following effects may be felt...'): euphoria, uncontrolled laughter; FRANK list after 'Taking nitrous oxide can cause:': 'feelings of euphoria, relaxation and calmness' and 'fits of giggles and laughter – hence the nickname laughing gas'.

Stays near ADF's sentence ('Dentists and medical professionals use it to sedate patients having minor medical procedures': four words in a row shared) but is not its wording. 'Doctors' is narrower than ADF's 'medical professionals'; pain relief is from ADF's first sentence ('commonly used for sedation and pain relief').

ADF: 'found in pressurised metal canisters' ('What does it look like?' and 'Other names' are sub-headings of 'What is nitrous oxide?'); FRANK's 'Also called' line has Balloons, Laughing Gas, Nos. 'Nangs' rests on ADF only.

pcp.line: PCP (phencyclidine) is a lab-made dissociative drug, created as an anaesthetic but no longer used as one.
pcp.note: All five anchors confirmed. The line is NIDA's sentence with words left out ('...is a synthetic (lab-made) dissociative drug developed as an intravenous (I.V.) anesthetic that has been discontinued...': six words in a row), so it is reworded; it says the same and no more. NIDA says the anaesthetic was discontinued; FRANK says it 'was designed to stop people feeling pain during operations'.

FRANK's three sentences carry the whole line. The NIDA sentence quoted (entry 'Dissociative Drugs') and the ADF one are about feeling disconnected from body and environment, which the line does not say in those words; NIDA's own PCP entry on the same page ('How does PCP make people feel?': 'Altered perception of reality.') fits the line more closely.

pcp.line: It comes as a liquid, oil, powder, crystals or pills, and is also called angel dust.
pcp.note: All five anchors confirmed. The first half is FRANK's sentence with one word changed ('PCP can be an oil, liquid, powder, crystal or pill.': nine words in a row), so it is reworded; same forms, same name.
